html:
The telephone is a device that turns the voice into electric signals, sends them along a wire and turns them back into sound at the other end. Alexander Graham Bell patented it in the United States in 1876, though several inventors were working on the same idea.

Bell was a Scottish-born teacher of the deaf living in Boston, interested in how speech and hearing work. He filed his patent on the same day in February 1876 that Elisha Gray filed a notice for a similar design, which led to long legal fights. Antonio Meucci in New York and Philipp Reis in Germany had built earlier talking devices too. Bell's patent held up in court, and on 10 March 1876 he spoke the famous first words to his assistant: "Mr. Watson, come here, I want to see you."

The telephone built on the telegraph, which had already sent coded messages over wires for decades (see transatlantic telegraph cable). But the telephone let anyone talk directly, with no operator to translate. The Bell Telephone Company, founded in 1877, grew into AT&T, for decades the largest company in the world. Thomas Edison improved the microphone, and exchanges with switchboard operators, often young women, connected callers.

By 1900 there were well over a million telephones in the United States. The telephone changed how businesses ran, how cities grew and how people kept in touch. It led on to radio, mobile phones and the networks that became the ARPANET and the internet.
